nameStory: Netrium digitus gets its scientific name from the Latin word 'digitus' meaning finger, referring to its distinctive elongated, finger-like cell shape. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, some microscopy enthusiasts call it the 'finger algae' for this very reason.
description: Netrium digitus is a microscopic single-celled green algae that lives in freshwater environments throughout New England. Each individual cell is remarkably large for a single-celled organism, visible to the naked eye as tiny green specks in pond water. The cells are distinctively elongated and cylindrical, resembling tiny green fingers or sausages when viewed under a magnifying glass or microscope. **Note: This description is based on general knowledge of the genus Netrium, as specific details about N. digitus are uncertain.**

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are distinctly finger-like or cylindrical, much longer than they are wide, appearing as tiny green rods floating in water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large enough to see as individual green specks with the naked eye, but details require magnification - typically several times longer than wide

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green due to chloroplasts, often appearing as a greenish tint in pond water when present in numbers

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Cells drift freely in water without active swimming, moving only with water currents - no flagella or visible locomotion

habitat: Found in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow-moving streams, and bog pools throughout New England's lowlands and mountains. Prefers slightly acidic, nutrient-poor waters and is often found in association with sphagnum moss and other bog plants.

seasonality.spring: Begins to multiply as water warms, becoming more noticeable in pond samples by late spring when growth accelerates.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when cells divide most rapidly and are easiest to spot in water samples.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as temperatures drop, but cells remain active until first frost in most New England locations.
seasonality.winter: Survives under ice in dormant state, nearly impossible to observe until spring warming begins the growth cycle again.

funFact: Despite being just a single cell, Netrium digitus is large enough to see individual cells with your naked eye - making it one of the few microorganisms you can actually spot without any magnification when looking closely at pond water!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other single-celled green algae, but the distinctly elongated finger-like shape sets it apart from round Chlorella or spiral Spirogyra. Remember: if it looks like a tiny green hot dog floating in pond water, it's likely a Netrium species.
contextualKnowledge: **Important note: Detailed information about this specific species is limited, and some identification features described here are based on general characteristics of the Netrium genus. Positive identification typically requires microscopic examination by someone familiar with freshwater algae.**
compareHints: Netrium digitus differs from its close relative N. oblongum primarily in cell proportions and internal structure details that require microscopic examination. Both species share the characteristic elongated cell shape, but digitus tends to have a more pronounced finger-like appearance. **Note: Distinguishing between Netrium species requires expertise in algal identification.**
